source: A digital signal sends information as separate values (0s and 1s), which can still be read exactly after some noise is added.
Students think "digital" just means electronic, rather than sent as distinct values.

A wave can carry information: a radio song, a phone call, a photo. There are two ways to code it. An analog signal copies the original smoothly, with every in-between value. A digital signal sends only a few separate values, usually just two: 0 and 1.

A digital signal sends information as distinct values (bits, 0 or 1). Because there are only a few allowed values, the receiver can still read every bit exactly after some noise is added, and copies can be perfect. With $n$ bits you can send $2^n$ different values.

Suppose 0 is sent as 0 volts and 1 as 5 volts. Noise on the way might turn 5 V into 4.3 V or 0 V into 0.6 V, but the receiver only asks "closer to 0 or to 5?" and recovers the exact bits. An analog signal has no such rule: every bit of noise becomes part of the signal, and copying a copy makes it worse each time.
An analog signal sampled into 3-bit numbers, sent as 0s and 1s with noise added, and read back exactly.
How many different values can a 4-bit signal send?
A receiver uses 0 V for 0 and 5 V for 1. It gets 4.6 V, 0.8 V, 4.1 V, 0.3 V. What bits were sent?
Anything closer to 5 V than to 0 V (above 2.5 V) is a 1; below is a 0.

Thinking "digital" just means electronic. An old analog radio is electronic too. Digital means the information is sent as separate, countable values rather than a smoothly varying wave. Check: can the signal only take a few set values? Then it is digital.
